name: Handyman
summary: Start a handyman business: your first 25 neighbors and partners, a price menu from real ranges, a punch list quote from a pasted list of jobs, and the licensed-trade rules to check in your state.
door_step3: I fix it, clean up and show you each job
door_rule: Door hangers go on the door, never in or on a mailbox: putting unstamped flyers in a mailbox is a federal offense (18 U.S. Code 1725). Check your city rules on door to door flyers.

promises.first_25: 15 people you know and 10 local agents, property managers, landlords and hardware stores, each with a message, plus door hangers.
promises.offer: Your price menu for visits and common jobs, the first-clients ladder, add-ons and job math, on a one-page offer sheet.
promises.quote: Which visit or job, how many and any extra hours in; a quote, a text and an invoice out.
promises.keep: A thank-you, an honest review ask, a referral ask and a later check-in, each dated, plus review cards with your QR code.
promises.sample_one: A free demo for one street or one partner business: door hangers or a sample letter, a card to send and every message, saved to your Pipeline.
promises.reply: Paste what someone wrote back: what they meant, a short answer with one next step, and your Pipeline updated. A draft you send yourself.
promises.won: Log the yes, then everything for the job: the booking text, a prep text, a printable job sheet, the after-job text and the invoice.
promises.proof: One finished punch list turned into proof: a result card, a before-and-after collage, a caption, an honest review ask and a case study once they say yes.
promises.next_25: The next 25 agents, property managers, landlords and hardware stores near you, not yet in your Pipeline, with messages for Do my day.
promises.ready: Look ready before you reach out: a one-page website, a Google profile kit and a flyer, all from your real prices.
promises.same_street: One customer's street turned into a route: door hangers with a neighbor price, a sheet for the 20 nearest homes and an intro ask for your customer.
promises.punch_list: A pasted list of small jobs in; hours, the order to do them, what goes to a licensed trade with your state's rule, and a printable estimate out.

crowd.note: Handyman work runs all year; spring and fall bring seasonal checkups (Housecall Pro) and the weatherstripping check (Fixr). The busier months are a judgment call.

Don't buy big tools before a job calls for them: rent or borrow the first time.

licenses.disclaimer: General information, not legal advice. Rules differ by state, county and city: check your state and city before you quote.

items.what_to_check: City or county license; state registration for an LLC; a DBA if you use a trade name.

sources.says: The licenses and permits you need from the state, county, or city will depend on your business activities and business location. You will have to research your own state, county, and city regulations.

items.item: Your state's limit for work without a contractor license
items.what_to_check: Many states let you take small jobs without a contractor license only under a dollar limit, and some only when no permit is needed. California is under $1,000 in labor and materials with no permit and no employees (CSLB). Arizona and Nevada are under $1,000 (A.R.S. 32-1121, NRS 624.031). Florida is under $2,500 (F.S. 489.103), Utah under $7,000 (Utah Code 58-55-305), and Virginia up to $1,000 (Code of Virginia 54.1-1100). In California, Arizona and Nevada your ads must say you're not licensed. Oregon requires a CCB license once you advertise, even with business cards (ORS 701.010). Check your state.

sources.says: Starting January 1, 2025 the minor work exemption is $1,000 (it was $500), but the work cannot require a permit and the unlicensed person cannot employ anyone; unlicensed individuals can advertise for work up to $1,000 if the ad says they are not licensed.

Exempt: one project with an aggregate contract price, including labor, materials and all other items, under $1,000, of a casual or minor nature; not if it needs a local building permit, is split to evade the chapter, or the ads don't say "not a licensed contractor".

489.103(9) (2026): the exemption covers casual, minor or inconsequential work with an aggregate contract price for labor, materials and all other items under $2,500; not for a person who advertises as a contractor.
58-55-305(1)(h): alteration or repair of a building under $7,000 including labor and materials is exempt, but plumbing, electrical, gas appliance and HVAC work go to licensed or certified people.
ORS 701.010(4): the exemption for casual, minor or inconsequential work under $1,000 does not apply to a person who advertises or puts out any sign or card that might indicate they are a contractor.

sources.publisher: California Business and Professions Code 7027.2 (via california.public.law)
sources.says: A person exempt under 7048 may advertise work under $1,000 only if the ad states that the person is not licensed under the Contractors State License Law.

NRS 624.031(6): any work to repair or maintain property the value of which is less than $1,000, including labor and materials, is exempt unless a building permit is required, the work is of a type performed by a plumbing, electrical, refrigeration, heating or air-conditioning contractor, or of a type performed by a contractor in a classification the Board prescribes that significantly affects the health, safety and welfare of the public, or it is part of a larger project of $500 or more or split to evade the chapter.

It is unlawful for any person, including a person exempt under NRS 624.031, to advertise as a contractor unless the person has a license in the appropriate classification; any person not licensed who advertises to perform construction work must state in the advertisement that he or she is not licensed.

Class C contractors perform or manage construction, removal, repair or improvements when the total value of a single contract or project is over $1,000 but less than $30,000; the Board requires a master tradesman license for electrical, plumbing and HVAC contractors.

items.what_to_check: Panels, new circuits, moved outlets, gas lines and appliances, moved pipes and heating and cooling systems go to a licensed trade in most states. Some states require a licensed electrician or plumber even to swap a fixture, faucet or switch (Nevada, Oregon, Utah and Virginia, and Florida for electrical work). Check your state.

sources.says: Plumbing and electrical work on a small project goes to a licensed contractor, or a licensed journeyman for a component such as a faucet, toilet, fixture, outlet or switch; HVAC to a licensed HVAC contractor.
NRS 624.031(6): repair or upkeep under $1,000 is exempt unless it needs a permit or is work of a type performed by a plumbing, electrical, refrigeration, heating or air-conditioning contractor.

Your state's law may require a licensed contractor for some work; specific trades that may need one include HVAC, plumbing, roofing, electrical installation and repair, concrete and masonry, and flooring.

sources.publisher: ORS 479.620 and 479.530 (Oregon Revised Statutes, via oregon.public.law)
sources.says: A person may not make any electrical installation without a supervising or journeyman electrician's license (or a limited residential electrician's license for dwellings); an electrical installation includes the maintenance or repair of installed wiring and permanently attached electrical products (ORS 479.530(10)). ORS 479.540 has no exemption for paid work on someone else's home, and OAR 918-282-0110 exempts only bulbs, fuses, plugging in portable equipment and a few low-voltage systems (single smoke detectors, intercoms, antennas, cameras).

sources.publisher: ORS 447.060 and 447.072 (Oregon Revised Statutes, via oregon.public.law)
sources.says: The plumbing license rules don't apply to a person doing plumbing work when not engaged for hire (447.060(1)(a)); plumbing includes installing, altering or repairing fixtures (447.010(6)); the permit and inspection exemption for ordinary minor repairs is available only to licensed plumbing contractors and persons described in ORS 693.020 (447.072).

A tradesman is any individual who engages in, or offers to engage in, work for the general public for compensation in the electrical, plumbing and HVAC trades (54.1-1128); no individual may work as a tradesman without a license, except under a licensed tradesman's supervision (54.1-1129(A)). Neither section has a dollar threshold.
489.503 (2026) has no exemption for unlicensed persons doing minor electrical work for pay.

items.what_to_check: Unlicensed work on any project that needs a building permit is illegal in California (CSLB). Cities list what needs no permit: Cotati lists fixture, fan, outlet and switch swaps and faucet and toilet repairs. Check your city.

sources.says: It is illegal for an unlicensed person to perform contracting work on any project which requires a building permit, or where labor and materials together come to $1,000 or more.

Work exempt from a building permit includes replacing light fixtures or ceiling fans, outlet replacements, switch replacements in existing boxes, faucet or toilet repair or replacement, and clearing stoppages without replacing valves or pipes. Updated 6/18/2025.

items.item: Lead-safe work in homes built before 1978
items.what_to_check: Paid work that disturbs more than 6 square feet of paint in a room, or 20 outside, or any window replacement, in a pre-1978 home needs an EPA- or state-certified firm and renovator. Ask what year the home was built.

sources.says: Jobs that disturb six square feet or less of paint per room inside, or 20 square feet or less on the exterior, are not covered; window replacement and demolition of painted surfaces are always covered; this includes all firms, even sole proprietorships.

Minor repair and maintenance activities, including minor electrical work and plumbing, disrupt 6 square feet or less of painted surface per room inside or 20 square feet or less outside, and do not involve window replacement or demolition of painted surfaces.

items.what_to_check: Scratched floors, a dropped TV, a leak after a faucet swap. Some states also require other insurance.

steps: Before the job: the price in writing from the Punch list quote, what's in it and what goes to a licensed trade, the year the home was built, and who buys the parts.
On arrival: walk the list with the owner, confirm each job and the price before you start, and point out anything that needs a licensed pro.
Photograph each spot before you touch it.
Patch the walls first so they can dry; turn the water off once for all the plumbing and the breaker off once for all the fixtures.
Ladders: 3 feet above the landing, the foot a quarter of the length out, never on a stepladder's top step (OSHA).
Anchor TVs, bookcases and dressers to the wall (CPSC).
If you find hidden damage, stop and explain the options before doing extra work. Take the after photos and invoice the same day.

sources.says: Small holes take 30 to 60 minutes of active work; plan for a total window of 24 hours before sanding and painting.

Portable ladders used to reach an upper landing extend at least 3 feet above it; a non-self-supporting ladder is set so the foot is about one-quarter of the working length out from the top support; the top step of a stepladder is not used as a step; ladders near exposed energized electrical equipment have nonconductive side rails.
Anchor TVs and furniture like bookcases and dressers securely to the wall.
Suggested estimate language: if we find hidden damage or the scope changes, I'll explain the options before doing extra work. Put change orders in writing before adding scope.

job_checklist.note: Walking the list, the photos and grouping the water and power jobs are common practice, a judgment call.

objections.objection: Can't I just do it myself?
objections.answer: Fair, and some people do. Thumbtack's advice is to group small jobs into one visit, since a single 20-minute job is often billed as a full hour. With you, the whole list is done in one visit at a price set before you start.

sources.says: Handymen who charge an hourly rate will often have a minimum charge: even if the task takes 20 minutes, you are likely to be charged for a full hour. Group together smaller household jobs.

objections.say: That's fair, and plenty of it is doable. If the list has been sitting for a while, I can knock it all out in one visit and you get the price before I start. Want to send me the list so you can compare?

objections.objection: Can you do the electrical panel (or gas line, or move the outlet) too?
objections.answer: No: panels, new wiring, moved outlets, gas lines and moved pipes go to a licensed electrician, plumber or gas fitter in most places. Say so plainly and offer to do the rest of the list.

sources.says: A building permit is required for panel replacement, adding a sub-panel, service upgrades and any changes to the electrical, gas, mechanical or plumbing systems, including relocating receptacles.

Some states cap the dollar value of jobs you can take without a contractor license ($500 to $10,000 or more, depending on the state); if the job crosses into licensed trade work, refer it out or partner with a licensed pro.

objections.say: That part needs a licensed pro where we are, so I don't take it on. I'm happy to do everything else on the list and work around their visit. Want me to price the rest?

objections.answer: By the time the list takes at your hourly rate, the way Housecall Pro suggests for a full punch list, with a trip minimum, parts extra and the price set before you start.

Handyman hourly rates run $50 to $80 for self-employed pros and $75 to $125 for companies; a minimum service fee of $125 to $200 covers travel, setup, admin and up to one hour of labor.

objections.say: I add up the time your whole list takes and price it as one visit, so small jobs cost less together than one at a time. Parts are extra and you get the price before I start. Send me the list and I'll price it today.

objections.answer: Say what you control: photos before you start, drop cloths, and stopping to ask before any extra work. Mention insurance only if you have it.

Suggested estimate language: if we find hidden damage or the scope changes, I'll explain the options before doing extra work. Put change orders in writing before adding scope.

objections.say: Good question. I take photos before I start, cover the floors and stop to ask before any extra work. [Your insurance, in one line, only if you have it.] Want me to take a look this week?

objections.answer: Not for most jobs. In a home built before 1978, work that disturbs more than a small patch of paint, or any window replacement, falls under EPA's lead-safe rule: ask the year and say what you can do.

sources.says: Jobs that disturb six square feet or less of paint per room inside, or 20 square feet or less on the exterior, are not covered; window replacement and demolition of painted surfaces are always covered; this includes all firms, even sole proprietorships.

Minor repair and maintenance activities, including minor electrical work and plumbing, disrupt 6 square feet or less of painted surface per room inside or 20 square feet or less outside, and do not involve window replacement or demolition of painted surfaces.

objections.say: Not for most of the list. What year was it built? If it's before 1978, I keep paint work small, and the bigger patches and any window replacement go to a lead-safe certified pro.

ladder.label: Founding price
ladder.ask: Permission to post before and after photos of the work (no faces, house numbers or license plates) and honest feedback, good or bad, that you may quote as from a founding client.

ladder.label: Early price
ladder.ask: Same work, a smaller discount, for customers 4 to 10.

ladder.label: Full price

ladder_note: Judgment call. The founding price is for being among your first 3 clients. In return you ask for honest feedback you may quote as from a founding client and permission to post before and after photos. Reviews are asked for after every job with nothing attached (Google bans any incentive; the FTC rule at 16 CFR 465 bans paying for positive ones).

keep.rules: Ask every customer for a review, happy or not, and never offer a discount, gift or anything else for one; Google's rules forbid it. Only share photos the customer said yes to.

advice.say: Faucet swap: same spot, same supply lines. Moving lines, new valves or new sink holes go to a licensed plumber, and some states require one even for a swap (Nevada, Oregon, Utah and Virginia). Check your state.
TV mounting: into studs or the right anchors, and no new outlet or power behind the wall: that is electrical work. CPSC: anchor TVs and furniture to the wall.
Anchor dressers, bookcases and tall pieces to the wall with the kit that comes with them (CPSC).
A patch dries before it is sanded and painted: plan a short second visit. In a home built before 1978, more than 6 square feet of paint in a room falls under EPA's lead-safe rule.
Housecall Pro: don't discount recurring work so far that you do more visits for less, so the plan keeps your full visit price.

street.headline: One small fix free on {street}
side: Sticky door, loose handle or a picture hung
includes: A sticky door, a loose handle or a picture hung
how: Text me your address and the fix
I stop by while I'm on {street}{day_part}
You see what the rest of your list would cost
street.line: I'm working on {street}{day_part}, so the first 3 neighbors who text me get one small fix free, about 15 minutes: a sticky door, a loose handle or a picture hung. No cost and no catch. No electrical, plumbing or gas.
street.post: Hi neighbors! I'm {first}, I run {business} here in {area}. I'm working on {street}{day_part}, so the first 3 neighbors who text me get one small fix free, about 15 minutes. No cost and no catch. {phone_line}
steps: Hang the door hangers on {street} the day before, on the door, never in or on a mailbox.
Do the first 3 fixes that are texted, with a photo before and after.
Hand each neighbor your price sheet and offer to price the rest of their list.
Text a thank-you the same day with the photo, then one follow-up in 3 days.

realtors.headline: The punch list done before the listing photos
steps: Send the message and the card today.
Ask which listing has a punch list and the photo day.
Do only the jobs the seller confirms in writing, and photograph before and after from the same spot.
Send the agent the photos the same day.

property_managers.card_line: For units {biz} manages: book through your property manager.
steps: Send the message and the card today.
Ask which unit turns over next and the day it must be ready.
Do only the jobs the manager confirms in writing, then photograph each one.
Send the photos the same day for their file.

landlords.card_line: Ask the office to book a visit.
steps: Send the message and the card today, or stop by the office.
Ask the owner or manager for the open small repair requests.
Do only what they confirm in writing, with before and after photos.
Send the photos the same day.

hardware_stores.demo: a free 30-minute how-to demo at your store, like hanging a heavy mirror
hardware_stores.headline: Bought the parts? I can put them in
steps: Send the message and the card today, or ask for the manager at the counter.
Offer the demo on a slow morning they pick.
Leave cards only where the manager says yes.
Thank them the same day.

same_street.neighbor_note: judgment call, not a sourced fact
same_street.headline: Your neighbor price on {street}
includes: Small hardware like screws and anchors
how: Text me your address and your list
You get the price before I start
same_street.customer_ask: Hi {customer}, thanks again! I'm working on {street}{day_part} and have time for a couple more homes. If a neighbor ever asks who fixed your list, would you pass on my number{phone_part}? It means a lot to a new business.
steps: Hang a door hanger on every home on this sheet the day before you work there. On the door, never in or on a mailbox.
While you work, say hi to anyone outside. Keep it short, and never say which neighbor: "I'm doing some repairs for a home on your street."
Text your customer the intro ask after the job, never before.
Mark each home on the sheet. A neighbor who books goes on the same day as your customer, while you're on the street.
same_street.why: When you are already on the street with your tools, a neighbor's list adds little driving, so you can give neighbors a better price on the same day.
